primitives.name: Signed Measure Subtraction Convention
primitives.verbatim_quote: To avoid the difficulty of indeterminate forms, we shall agree to subtract two measures only if at least one of them is finite.
primitives.assumptions: Measurable space (X,S); μ1, μ2 are measures; at least one of μ1(E) or μ2(E) is finite for any measurable set E.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Indeterminate form ∞ - ∞ when both measures are infinite.

primitives.name: Measure Difference Representation
primitives.verbatim_quote: One of our objectives in the following study is to prove that every signed measure is the difference of two measures.
primitives.assumptions: Signed measure μ defined on measurable space (X,S); μ assumes at most one of ±∞.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Singularity occurs when both positive and negative variations are unbounded.

layer2.mapping: GSI: Every signed likelihood ratio can be decomposed into a pair of competing priors. GSE: A signed state transition kernel can be split into forward and backward probability flows.
layer2.telemetry: Observation of balanced probability flows in Markov chain Monte Carlo kernels

primitives.verbatim_quote: For instance, a signed measure μ is totally finite if X is measurable and | μ(X) < ∞.
primitives.assumptions: μ is a signed measure on (X,S); X is measurable.

The foundational challenge is handling signed measures whose positive and negative parts may both be infinite, leading to indeterminate forms. The subtraction convention resolves this by requiring at least one component to be finite, mirroring the rule for Lebesgue integration where f = g - h with at least one integrable part. This leads to the fundamental representation theorem: every signed measure μ can be written as μ = μ+ - μ-, where μ+ and μ- are mutually singular measures obtained via the Hahn decomposition. This decomposition is unique up to sets of measure zero. In applications, this translates directly: in GSI, a signed likelihood ratio μ = dQ/dP is integrable exactly when the Kullback-Leibler divergence D(P||Q) is finite; in GSE, a signed Markov kernel K(x,dy) = p+(x,y)dy - p-(x,y)dy must satisfy ∫|K(x,dy)| < ∞ for all x to ensure bounded linear operators on Banach spaces.
